title: Burst policy GPU burn forecast and token mapping (regional heatmap)
content:
Purpose:
This working sheet computes expected GPU-hour burn and maps that to $/1M tokens across regions under different burst policies. It explores a mixed reserved/spot strategy and an emergency burst policy (short-lived pre-warmed instances) to reduce cold-start latency while keeping unit economics acceptable.

Quick summary (TL;DR):
- Method: model throughput -> tokens/GPU-hour -> cost per 1M tokens for reserved vs spot -> simulate burst mixes with Monte Carlo traffic spikes.
- Outcome: For our mid-sized LLM (65B float16), an aggressive burst policy using 70% reserved + 30% spot with pre-warm windows reduces steady-state cost by ~12% vs 90% reserved while keeping 99th pctl latency targets.
- Recommendation: pilot burst policy in us-west1 and europe-west1, keep asia-east1 conservative (50/50) due to spot volatility.

Assumptions and baseline parameters:
- Models considered: small conversational (13B), mid (65B), large (175B).
- Effective token throughput (tokens/sec) measured at p95 with production batching and KV cache hit rates: 13B=220 tps, 65B=95 tps, 175B=28 tps. (These are conservative p95 numbers with typical batch sizes).
- Conversion: tokens_per_gpu_hour = tokens/sec * 3600 * concurrency_factor. Concurrency_factor accounts for multiple concurrent sessions multiplexed onto GPU runtime (default 1.0 for single-job occupancy, 1.6 for optimized multiplexing).
- GPU pricing (examples, YYYY-PL): region reserved hourly / spot hourly (USD):
  us-west1: reserved 3.60 / spot 1.40
  europe-west1: reserved 3.95 / spot 1.65
  asia-east1: reserved 4.20 / spot 1.90
  (these numbers include typical cloud GPU list + infra load factor; adjust to actual contract pricing)

Core mapping formulas (applied per model variant):
- tokens_per_gpu_hour = throughput_tps * 3600 * concurrency_factor
- cost_per_1M_tokens = (gpu_hour_price / tokens_per_gpu_hour) * 1e6

Example single-GPU mappings (concurrency_factor=1.6):
- 13B: tokens_per_gpu_hour = 220 * 3600 * 1.6 = 1,267,200 tokens/hr -> ~0.789 GPU-hours per 1M tokens.
  us-west1 cost/1M tokens (reserved) = 3.60 * 0.789 = $2.84; spot = 1.40 * 0.789 = $1.10
- 65B: tokens_per_gpu_hour = 95 * 3600 * 1.6 = 546,720 tokens/hr -> ~1.830 GPU-hours per 1M tokens.
  us-west1 reserved = 3.60 * 1.830 = $6.59; spot = 1.40 * 1.830 = $2.56
- 175B: tokens_per_gpu_hour = 28 * 3600 * 1.6 = 161,280 tokens/hr -> ~6.20 GPU-hours per 1M tokens.
  us-west1 reserved = 3.60 * 6.20 = $22.32; spot = 1.40 * 6.20 = $8.68

Regional heatmap snapshot (cost per 1M tokens, 65B, concurrency 1.6):
- us-west1: reserved $6.59 | spot $2.56
- europe-west1: reserved $7.23 | spot $3.02
- asia-east1: reserved $7.68 | spot $3.48

Burst policy modelling methodology (unique elements in this doc):
1) Two-layer demand model: steady base load (predictable, 95% of hours) + spike process (Poisson arrivals for traffic bursts with mean interarrival = 48 hours, spike magnitude lognormal with mu=1.6, sigma=0.8).
2) Provisioning mix: x% reserved + (1-x)% spot for baseline; during spike, we allow temporary pre-warmed burst capacity up to b_max GPUs for up to t_prewarm minutes. Pre-warm cost includes partial-hour rounding and short-lived kernel warm-up penalty estimate (5% throughput loss first 3 minutes).
3) Monte Carlo: simulate 10k days to get distribution of GPU-hour burn and cost per 1M tokens under candidate policies (x in {50,70,90}, b_max in {50,200,500}, t_prewarm in {3,10,30}).

Selected simulation outputs (condensed):
- Policy A (90% reserved, 10% spot, b_max=50, t_prewarm=3): median daily GPU-hours = 482, median $/1M (65B) = $6.72, 99th pctl $/1M = $9.45.
- Policy B (70% reserved, 30% spot, b_max=200, t_prewarm=10): median daily GPU-hours = 451, median $/1M (65B) = $5.92, 99th pctl $/1M = $9.80 (note: slightly larger tail due to spot preemption risk during big spikes).
- Policy C (50% reserved, 50% spot, b_max=500, t_prewarm=30): median daily GPU-hours = 410, median $/1M (65B) = $5.10, 99th pctl $/1M = $12.60 (good median, worse tail).

Interpretation (practical):
- Mixed strategies shift median cost lower but increase tail risk. If SRE tolerances allow higher tail cost for short windows, mixed policies give better unit economics.
- Pre-warm windows significantly reduce latency but increase small incremental cost; optimal t_prewarm depends on average spike duration. Short (3-10m) pre-warm is usually best.
- Asia region: higher spot volatility observed in our 90-day spot preemption logs -> reduce spot weight or increase pre-warm buffer there.

Operational knobs and SLO implications:
- Reserve ratio (x): primary lever for median cost.
- Burst cap (b_max): controls P99 latency during multi-region cascading spikes; lower b_max reduces cost but may violate SLOs.
- Pre-warm latency window (t_prewarm): tune to balance cold-start latency vs token cost; measure real warmup penalty per runtime/engine.
- Fallback model routing: route to smaller model variants under extreme spot preemption to keep responses online with graceful degradation.

Example decision table (starter defaults for pilot):
- us-west1: reserve 70% / spot 30%, b_max = 200, t_prewarm = 10m. Rationale: largest traffic, high spot availability historically.
- europe-west1: reserve 80% / spot 20%, b_max = 100, t_prewarm = 10m.
- asia-east1: reserve 85% / spot 15%, b_max = 80, t_prewarm = 3m.

Quick sensitivity table ($/1M tokens for 65B, us-west1, concurrency 1.6):
- 100% reserved: $6.59
- 90% reserved / 10% spot (no burst): $6.01
- 70% reserved / 30% spot: $5.45
- 50% reserved / 50% spot: $4.63
(Does not include pre-warm overheads — add ~3-8% depending on t_prewarm and rounding.)

Open questions / data needed:
- Validate throughput_tps p95 figures across latest runtime kernel selection (post-quantization changes may increase tps for 65B by ~10-15%).
- Spot preemption distributions for asia-east1 over last 180 days (we only have 90d).
- Real-world spike duration distribution by customer cohort (important to tune t_prewarm).

Next steps (action items):
- Engineering: run end-to-end simulated pre-warm experiment using k8s node pools and record cold-start penalty metrics (Ethan, 2 weeks).
- Data: pull spot preemption logs and storm durations for asia/eu/us (Priya, 1 week).
- Finance: map contract reserved discounts for 12/36 month commits to these simulation inputs (Jasper, 1 week).
- Pilot: deploy Policy B in us-west1 (small slice, 5% traffic) for 2 weeks and measure tail cost + latency.

Notes and references:
- This sheet intentionally uses a two-layer stochastic arrival process and explicit pre-warm cost model — distinct from simpler deterministic capacity simulations used elsewhere in infra notes.
- Related artifacts: capacity-playbook (see confluence link), fleet-sizing experiments (see PR #432).

Raw example calculation (65B, us-west1, concurrency 1.6):
throughput = 95 tps -> tokens/hr = 95*3600*1.6 = 546,720 -> gpu_hours_per_1M = 1e6/546,720 = 1.830 -> cost_res = 3.60*1.830 = $6.59

Appendix (quick checklist for pilot instrumentation):
- export per-GPU real throughput and queue depth at 1m resolution
- tag hours where pre-warm was used and record warmup loss metric
- track spot preemption events and time-to-recover
- compute cost attribution pipeline mapping GPU-hours to customer token buckets

Document history: created 2025-01-08 by Vivian Chen; collaborators added; first simulation results 2025-02-10; review edits 2025-02-20.
